Student Sleep Quality¶

Zack Mitra & Rene Franceschini | Project Website

As technology advances so does our way of communicating, social media has been an incredibly large and growing industry. The increase of availability towards social media arises questions of whether or not it affects common aspects of life. In this case, we will be investigating if social media affects sleep quality.

Central Research Questions¶

  1. Is there a screen time threshold (a "cutoff") beyond which sleep quality and duration measurably decline? We hypothesize that there is a non-linear tipping point. Moderate screen use may not affect sleep, but heavy use does.
  2. Can we predict a student's sleep quality score and sleep duration from screen time, caffeine intake, and physical activity using a KNN model?

Why These Datasets?¶

We are using two Kaggle datasets:

Dataset Source Key Variables
Student Sleep Patterns arsalanjamal002 Age, Gender, Year, Sleep Duration, Screen Time, Caffeine, Study Hours, Sleep Quality
Sleep, Screen Time & Stress Analysis jayjoshi37 Screen Time, Sleep Hours, Stress Level, Sleep Score, Caffeine

Dataset 1 is student-focused (500 rows, undergraduates), providing academic context, year in school and study hours alongside sleep and lifestyle variables. Dataset 2 broadens coverage with a stress dimension and a derived sleep score, which gives us an even more practical target variable for our KNN model.

Together these datasets let us:

  • Validate trends across two independent samples
  • Build a merged feature space that includes screen time, caffeine, stress, and physical activity
  • Have enough statistical power to identify a screen-time cutoff reliably

Why the data is appropriate: Both datasets are observational survey datasets of individuals (students / general adults) measured on objective lifestyle metrics. There are no obvious selection biases that would invalidate our questions. The sample sizes (500+ each) are adequate for EDA and KNN modeling. The key shared variables — screen time in hours, sleep duration in hours, and caffeine intake — are consistently operationalized, making a merge tractable.

Tidy Data Principles Applied¶

Per Wickham (2014), tidy data requires:

  1. Each variable forms a column.
  2. Each observation forms a row.
  3. Each type of observational unit forms a table.

Both raw datasets already satisfy (1) and (2). Our cleaning steps enforce (3) by harmonizing column names, resolving missing values, dropping duplicates, and engineering a merged table ready for modeling.

2. Tidy the Data¶

The following steps clean and standardize both datasets before merging:

  • Rename columns to a common snake_case schema so shared variables are aligned.
  • Drop duplicates and rows where the key variables (screen time, sleep duration) are missing.
  • Enforce dtypes — numeric columns are cast to float; categorical columns to category.
  • Engineer derived columns where useful (e.g., screen_time_bin for cutoff analysis).
  • Merge into a single analysis-ready DataFrame for EDA.
In [37]:
# ── Tidy Dataset 1 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
df1 = df1_raw.copy()

# Standardize column names to lowercase snake_case
df1.columns = df1.columns.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(' ', '_')
print('Cleaned columns (df1):', list(df1.columns))

# Map to a universal schema
rename_map1 = {
    'sleep_duration':   'sleep_hours',
    'sleep_quality':    'sleep_quality',
    'screen_time':      'screen_time_hrs',
    'caffeine_intake':  'caffeine_mg',
    'physical_activity':'physical_activity_hrs',
    'study_hours':      'study_hours',
    'university_year':  'year',
    'gender':           'gender',
    'age':              'age',
}
df1.rename(columns={k: v for k, v in rename_map1.items() if k in df1.columns}, inplace=True)

# Keep only columns we need; add a source tag
cols1 = ['age','gender','year','sleep_hours','sleep_quality',
         'screen_time_hrs','caffeine_mg','physical_activity_hrs','study_hours']
cols1 = [c for c in cols1 if c in df1.columns]
df1 = df1[cols1].copy()
df1['source'] = 'student_patterns'

# Drop duplicates and rows missing the two key variables
before = len(df1)
df1.drop_duplicates(inplace=True)
df1.dropna(subset=['sleep_hours','screen_time_hrs'], inplace=True)
print(f'Rows after cleaning df1: {before} → {len(df1)}')

# Enforce numeric types
for col in ['sleep_hours','sleep_quality','screen_time_hrs','caffeine_mg','physical_activity_hrs']:
    if col in df1.columns:
        df1[col] = pd.to_numeric(df1[col], errors='coerce')

# ── Merge ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
df = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True, sort=False)

# ── Engineer derived columns ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Screen time bins (for cutoff analysis)
df['screen_time_bin'] = pd.cut(
    df['screen_time_hrs'],
    bins=[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 24],
    labels=['0–2 hrs','2–4 hrs','4–6 hrs','6–8 hrs','8+ hrs'],
    right=True
)

# Sleep quality category (low / medium / high — based on tertiles)
if 'sleep_quality' in df.columns:
    q1, q2 = df['sleep_quality'].quantile([0.33, 0.67])
    df['sleep_quality_cat'] = pd.cut(
        df['sleep_quality'],
        bins=[-np.inf, q1, q2, np.inf],
        labels=['Low','Medium','High']
    )

print(f'Merged DataFrame shape: {df.shape}')
print(f'Sources: {df["source"].value_counts().to_dict()}')
df.head()

4. Exploratory Data Analysis — 5 Graphs¶

Each graph below addresses one or more of our research questions. A Markdown summary immediately follows each figure explaining the key takeaway.

Graph 1 — Screen Time vs. Sleep Quality (Scatter + Regression Line)¶

Purpose: Directly probe whether more screen time is associated with lower sleep quality. The linear regression line and 95% confidence band show the overall trend; individual points are alpha-blended to reveal density.

Expected Finding: We expect a negative slope — as screen time rises, sleep quality falls — but likely with high variance, suggesting the relationship is moderated by other factors (caffeine, physical activity).

In [44]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

if 'sleep_quality' in df.columns:
    plot_df = df[['screen_time_hrs','sleep_quality']].dropna()
    ax.scatter(plot_df['screen_time_hrs'], plot_df['sleep_quality'],
               alpha=0.35, s=18, color='steelblue', label='Observations')

    # OLS regression line
    m, b, r, p, se = stats.linregress(plot_df['screen_time_hrs'], plot_df['sleep_quality'])
    x_line = np.linspace(plot_df['screen_time_hrs'].min(), plot_df['screen_time_hrs'].max(), 200)
    ax.plot(x_line, m * x_line + b, color='firebrick', linewidth=2,
            label=f'OLS fit  (r={r:.2f}, p={p:.3f})')
    ax.fill_between(x_line,
                    (m * x_line + b) - 1.96 * se * np.sqrt(len(plot_df)),
                    (m * x_line + b) + 1.96 * se * np.sqrt(len(plot_df)),
                    alpha=0.08, color='firebrick')

    ax.set_title('Screen Time vs. Sleep Quality', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('Daily Screen Time (hours)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Sleep Quality Score')
    ax.legend()
    print(f'Pearson r = {r:.3f}  |  p-value = {p:.4f}  |  Slope = {m:.4f}')
else:
    # Fallback: Screen Time vs Sleep Hours
    plot_df = df[['screen_time_hrs','sleep_hours']].dropna()
    ax.scatter(plot_df['screen_time_hrs'], plot_df['sleep_hours'],
               alpha=0.35, s=18, color='steelblue')
    m, b, r, p, se = stats.linregress(plot_df['screen_time_hrs'], plot_df['sleep_hours'])
    x_line = np.linspace(plot_df['screen_time_hrs'].min(), plot_df['screen_time_hrs'].max(), 200)
    ax.plot(x_line, m * x_line + b, color='firebrick', linewidth=2,
            label=f'OLS fit  (r={r:.2f}, p={p:.3f})')
    ax.set_title('Screen Time vs. Sleep Duration', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('Daily Screen Time (hours)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Sleep Duration (hours)')
    ax.legend()
    print(f'Pearson r = {r:.3f}  |  p-value = {p:.4f}')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('graph1_scatter.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()

Pearson r = -0.675  |  p-value = 0.0000  |  Slope = -0.4583

Takeaway (Graph 1): The regression slope and Pearson r tell us the direction and magnitude of the screen–sleep relationship. A statistically significant negative r would confirm Hypothesis 1. Even a modest effect here matters practically: for students already sleep-deprived, small additional sleep loss accumulates.

Graph 2 — Mean Sleep Quality / Duration by Screen Time Bin (Bar Chart with Error Bars)¶

Purpose: Identify the screen-time cutoff — the bin where the mean sleep metric first drops meaningfully below the low-usage baseline. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals, so we can assess which differences are statistically reliable.

Why a bar chart? Comparing a continuous outcome across an ordinal categorical variable is the classic use case for a grouped bar chart. The bins (0–2 hrs, 2–4 hrs, …) operationalize our cutoff question directly.

In [45]:
target = 'sleep_quality' if 'sleep_quality' in df.columns else 'sleep_hours'
ylabel = 'Mean Sleep Quality Score' if target == 'sleep_quality' else 'Mean Sleep Duration (hrs)'

group_means = (
    df.groupby('screen_time_bin', observed=True)[target]
    .agg(['mean','sem','count'])
    .reset_index()
)
group_means['ci95'] = group_means['sem'] * 1.96

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
bars = ax.bar(
    group_means['screen_time_bin'].astype(str),
    group_means['mean'],
    yerr=group_means['ci95'],
    capsize=5,
    color=sns.color_palette('Blues_d', len(group_means)),
    edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.7
)

# Annotate count per bar
for bar, row in zip(bars, group_means.itertuples()):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
            bar.get_height() + row.ci95 + 0.05,
            f'n={int(row.count)}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8, color='gray')

ax.set_title(f'{ylabel} by Screen Time Bin\n(Error bars = 95% CI)', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel('Daily Screen Time Bin')
ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('graph2_bar.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()
print(group_means[['screen_time_bin','mean','ci95','count']].round(3).to_string(index=False))

screen_time_bin  mean  ci95  count
        0–2 hrs 7.912 0.072   1832
        2–4 hrs 7.294 0.051   3671
        4–6 hrs 6.515 0.040   3382
        6–8 hrs 5.495 0.041   3266
         8+ hrs 4.516 0.040   3349

Takeaway (Graph 2): Look for the bin where the mean first drops outside the 95% CI of the 0–2 hrs baseline group. That bin is our empirical screen-time cutoff. If the means are flat across bins, it suggests screen time alone is insufficient to predict sleep quality and that confounders (caffeine, stress) must be included in the model.

Graph 5 — Screen Time vs. Sleep Quality, Split by Caffeine Level (Grouped Scatter / FacetGrid)¶

Purpose: Investigate the interaction between caffeine and screen time. Students who consume high caffeine and spend many hours on screens may experience compounded sleep disruption compared to those with only one risk factor.

Why a FacetGrid? Splitting the scatter by caffeine tertile preserves within-group regression lines, making the moderation effect (if any) visually apparent.

In [46]:
if 'caffeine_bin' in df.columns and 'sleep_quality' in df.columns:
    plot5_df = df.dropna(subset=['screen_time_hrs','sleep_quality','caffeine_bin'])

    g = sns.FacetGrid(plot5_df, col='caffeine_bin', height=4.5, aspect=0.9,
                      col_order=['Low Caffeine','Medium Caffeine','High Caffeine'])
    g.map_dataframe(sns.regplot, x='screen_time_hrs', y='sleep_quality',
                    scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.3, 's': 12}, line_kws={'color': 'firebrick'},
                    ci=95)
    g.set_titles('{col_name}', size=11)
    g.set_axis_labels('Screen Time (hrs)', 'Sleep Quality Score')
    g.figure.suptitle('Screen Time vs. Sleep Quality by Caffeine Level\n(Each panel = caffeine tertile)',
                       y=1.03, fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('graph5_facet.png', dpi=150)
    plt.show()

    # Print slope per group
    print('=== OLS Slope of Screen Time → Sleep Quality per Caffeine Group ===')
    for grp in ['Low Caffeine','Medium Caffeine','High Caffeine']:
        sub = plot5_df[plot5_df['caffeine_bin'] == grp][['screen_time_hrs','sleep_quality']].dropna()
        if len(sub) > 10:
            m, b, r, p, _ = stats.linregress(sub['screen_time_hrs'], sub['sleep_quality'])
            print(f'  {grp}: slope={m:.4f}, r={r:.3f}, p={p:.4f}, n={len(sub)}')

elif 'caffeine_mg' in df.columns:
    # Fallback: hue-colored scatter if no bins yet
    plot5_df = df.dropna(subset=['screen_time_hrs','sleep_hours','caffeine_mg'])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
    sc = ax.scatter(plot5_df['screen_time_hrs'], plot5_df['sleep_hours'],
                    c=plot5_df['caffeine_mg'], cmap='YlOrRd', alpha=0.4, s=18)
    plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label='Caffeine (mg)')
    ax.set_title('Screen Time vs. Sleep Duration\n(color = caffeine intake)', fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('Screen Time (hrs)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Sleep Duration (hrs)')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('graph5_scatter_caffeine.png', dpi=150)
    plt.show()

=== OLS Slope of Screen Time → Sleep Quality per Caffeine Group ===
  Low Caffeine: slope=-0.4645, r=-0.691, p=0.0000, n=6170
  Medium Caffeine: slope=-0.4585, r=-0.680, p=0.0000, n=6170
  High Caffeine: slope=-0.4459, r=-0.637, p=0.0000, n=3160

Takeaway (Graph 5): If the regression slope becomes steeper (more negative) in the High Caffeine panel compared to Low Caffeine, this is evidence of a caffeine–screen time interaction: caffeine amplifies the harm of screen time on sleep. This interaction term should then be included as an engineered feature in our KNN model.

5. Screen Time Cutoff Analysis¶

To formally identify a cutoff, we compute the mean sleep quality (or duration) for each screen-time bin and flag the first bin whose mean falls below a meaningful threshold (1 standard deviation below the overall mean). We also run pairwise t-tests between the low-usage group and each subsequent bin.

In [47]:
target = 'sleep_quality' if 'sleep_quality' in df.columns else 'sleep_hours'
overall_mean = df[target].mean()
overall_std  = df[target].std()
threshold    = overall_mean - 0.5 * overall_std

print(f'Overall mean {target}: {overall_mean:.3f}')
print(f'Cutoff threshold (mean – 0.5 SD): {threshold:.3f}')
print()

bin_order = ['0–2 hrs','2–4 hrs','4–6 hrs','6–8 hrs','8+ hrs']
baseline_grp = df[df['screen_time_bin'] == '0–2 hrs'][target].dropna()

print('=== Pairwise t-tests vs. Baseline (0–2 hrs) ===')
for b in bin_order[1:]:
    grp = df[df['screen_time_bin'] == b][target].dropna()
    if len(grp) > 5:
        t_stat, p_val = stats.ttest_ind(baseline_grp, grp, equal_var=False)
        flag = '  *** CUTOFF CANDIDATE ***' if grp.mean() < threshold else ''
        print(f'  {b}: mean={grp.mean():.3f}, t={t_stat:.3f}, p={p_val:.4f}{flag}')

# Visualize the cutoff threshold
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
group_means = (
    df.groupby('screen_time_bin', observed=True)[target]
    .agg(['mean','sem']).reset_index()
)
group_means['ci95'] = group_means['sem'] * 1.96
ax.errorbar(
    group_means['screen_time_bin'].astype(str),
    group_means['mean'],
    yerr=group_means['ci95'],
    fmt='o-', capsize=5, color='steelblue', linewidth=2, markersize=8
)
ax.axhline(threshold, color='firebrick', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label=f'Threshold (mean–0.5SD = {threshold:.2f})')
ax.axhline(overall_mean, color='gray', linestyle=':', linewidth=1.2, label=f'Overall mean = {overall_mean:.2f}')
ax.set_title(f'Mean {target} by Screen Time Bin with Cutoff Threshold', fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel('Screen Time Bin')
ax.set_ylabel(target.replace('_',' ').title())
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('graph_cutoff.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()

Overall mean sleep_quality: 6.218
Cutoff threshold (mean – 0.5 SD): 5.330

=== Pairwise t-tests vs. Baseline (0–2 hrs) ===

  4–6 hrs: mean=6.515, t=33.222, p=0.0000
  6–8 hrs: mean=5.495, t=57.261, p=0.0000
  8+ hrs: mean=4.516, t=80.906, p=0.0000  *** CUTOFF CANDIDATE ***

2 Plausible Models for Future Investigation¶

Model 1: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Regressor¶

  • Purpose: Predict a student's sleep quality based on their daily lifestyle habits.
  • Dependent Variable: sleep_quality (Continuous/Ordinal scale)
  • Independent Variables: screen_time_hrs, caffeine_mg, physical_activity_hrs, study_hours
  • Methodology: We will scale the features using StandardScaler. We will use a standard train/test split (80/20) and evaluate the model using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and R-squared ($R^2$). We will optimize the hyperparameter $k$ using cross-validation.

Model 2: Multiple Linear Regression¶

  • Purpose: To model the interaction effect between caffeine and screen time on sleep duration.
  • Dependent Variable: sleep_hours
  • Independent Variables: screen_time_hrs, caffeine_mg, and an interaction term (screen_time_hrs * caffeine_mg).
  • Methodology: We will fit an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression model. The EDA supports this by showing different regression slopes for different caffeine levels. We will test the statistical significance of the interaction coefficient to find whether caffeine compounds the negative effects of screen time.

7. Milestone 2 Summary & Conclusions¶

What We Did¶

  • Tidied both Kaggle datasets into a unified, analysis-ready DataFrame with consistent column names, enforced dtypes, no duplicates, and no missing values on key variables.
  • Posed and discussed three focused research questions connecting screen time, caffeine, and sleep outcomes.
  • Produced 5 EDA graphs covering: scatter regression (relationship direction), bar chart with CI (cutoff identification), violin+box (distribution shape), correlation heatmap (feature selection for KNN), and a faceted scatter by caffeine level (interaction effect).
  • Computed cross-tabulations of screen time bin × sleep quality category and caffeine tertile × sleep quality category.
  • Applied grouped statistics — means, medians, standard errors — by screen time bin.
  • Ran a baseline KNN model (k=5) as a proof-of-concept for Milestone 3.

Next Steps (Milestone 3)¶

  1. Hyperparameter tuning — grid search over k (1–25) with cross-validation to find the optimal KNN.
  2. Interactive widget — a Jupyter ipywidgets slider for screen time input that returns predicted sleep quality, sleep duration, and caffeine impact in real time.
  3. Formal cutoff analysis — a piecewise regression or LOWESS curve to estimate the non-linear screen-time threshold.
  4. Feature importance — permutation importance on the KNN to rank predictors.
  5. Website update — publish new graphs and model demo to the GitHub Pages site.
